sections.heading: What does anaemia feel like?
sections.body:
Many people with iron deficiency anaemia have only a few symptoms. Tiredness and a lack of energy are common, and some people also notice shortness of breath, a pounding heartbeat, paler skin or headaches. Less often there may be ringing in the ears, an altered sense of taste, hair loss, a craving to eat non-food items (called pica) or spoon-shaped nails. Low iron has also been linked with restless legs syndrome, even when anaemia is not fully present.

Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia can cause extreme tiredness, a sore red tongue, pins and needles and mouth ulcers. It can also cause muscle weakness and problems with vision, memory or judgement. The NHS says that the longer this type goes untreated, the higher the chance of permanent damage, and long-term B12 deficiency can damage nerves.

sections.heading: What are the main types of anaemia?
sections.body:
Iron deficiency is the most common type of anaemia, and vitamin B12 and folate deficiency are other frequent causes. MedlinePlus also lists anaemia of chronic disease, sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia and aplastic anaemia among the types. Anaemia of chronic disease is linked with long-term conditions such as kidney disease, cancer, ulcerative colitis or rheumatoid arthritis. Thalassaemia is inherited, while aplastic anaemia involves damage to the stem cells in the bone marrow that make blood cells.

In the UK, the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency is pernicious anaemia. In this condition the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach, so the body cannot absorb B12 from food. Diet can also contribute, particularly for vegetarians, and some medicines, including anticonvulsants and proton pump inhibitors, can reduce absorption. Folate deficiency can also follow heavy alcohol use or a raised need for folate, as in pregnancy.

sections.heading: What happens at an appointment, and which tests are used?
sections.body:
A GP usually asks about lifestyle and medical history and then arranges a blood test. This is a full blood count, which checks the red blood cells, and the GP may also test ferritin, a protein that stores iron. A low ferritin suggests that there is not much iron stored in the body.

Finding the cause matters because treatment depends on it. The GP may ask about diet, heavy periods and medicines such as ibuprofen or aspirin, which can cause bleeding in the stomach. In men and in women after the menopause, bleeding in the gut is the most common cause of iron deficiency, whereas in women before the menopause it is heavy periods. If the cause is unclear, further tests may follow, such as a stool sample test for blood, and testing for coeliac disease may be suggested. For vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, a GP can often make the diagnosis from symptoms and blood tests.

sections.heading: How is anaemia treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on the type of anaemia and its cause. Iron deficiency anaemia is usually treated with iron tablets and iron-rich foods, while the underlying cause, such as heavy periods or bleeding, is also addressed. Common side effects of iron tablets include constipation or diarrhoea, tummy pain, heartburn, feeling sick and darker than usual poo. Taking tablets with or shortly after food can help, and the GP may change how often they are taken. An iron infusion may be used when a person cannot take tablets or cannot absorb iron through the gut.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is usually treated with hydroxocobalamin injections, followed by tablets or continuing injections depending on the cause. When the deficiency is not caused by diet, injections may be needed long term. Folate deficiency is treated with folic acid tablets, and doctors check B12 first because folic acid can sometimes hide a B12 deficiency. A follow-up blood test is usually arranged to confirm that treatment is working. For other types, MedlinePlus says anaemia usually improves when the condition causing it is treated.

sections.heading: Living with anaemia and what to expect
sections.body:
Vitamin B12 is found in meat, fish, eggs, dairy products and fortified foods. Good sources of folate include broccoli, brussels sprouts, asparagus, peas, chickpeas and brown rice. Iron supplements should be kept out of the reach of children, because an overdose in a young child can be fatal.

Untreated iron deficiency anaemia may lead to heart problems, complications in pregnancy and delayed development in children. Delays in treating B12 deficiency can cause lasting nerve damage, so early diagnosis matters. Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia most often responds well to treatment. Sickle cell disease causes long-term anaemia with episodes of pain, and care focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications. Overall, the outlook depends on the condition causing the anaemia. Chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness at rest need an emergency call to 999, black or bloody stools need NHS 111 or a same-day GP call, and ongoing tiredness or paleness is a reason for a routine GP appointment.

faqs.q: Is anaemia the same as iron deficiency?
faqs.a: No, iron deficiency is only the most common type. Anaemia can also come from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, long-term conditions, inherited conditions such as sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, or aplastic anaemia. Treatment depends on the type, which is why a blood test comes first.

faqs.q: Why do doctors look for the cause of iron deficiency?
faqs.a: Finding the cause matters because treatment depends on it. In men and in women after the menopause, bleeding in the gut is the most common cause. Causes such as stomach ulcers or bowel cancer are considered, so a GP may arrange further tests if the reason is unclear.

faqs.q: Do iron tablets have side effects?
faqs.a: They can, and the NHS lists constipation or diarrhoea, tummy pain, heartburn, feeling sick and darker than usual poo. Taking them with or shortly after food can help. A GP may adjust how often the tablets are taken, and people with troublesome effects usually talk to the GP rather than stopping on their own.

faqs.q: Why might vitamin B12 be given by injection?
faqs.a: Injections are used when the problem is poor absorption, as in pernicious anaemia, where the immune system attacks healthy stomach cells. The NHS says hydroxocobalamin is the form used in the UK. When low B12 is only due to diet, tablets may be enough.

No, many people with iron deficiency anaemia have only a few symptoms. It can be found through a blood test done for another reason. Anyone who has symptoms such as persistent tiredness, paleness or breathlessness can book a routine GP appointment.
